title: Scaling Empowered Agents

Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Scaling Empowered Agents
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Empowerment measures the capacity of an agent to actively control its environment. In this work, we explain the connection between skill learning and empowerment. While skill learning is not empowerment, we introduce a simple scalable recipe for empowerment maximization: empowerment corresponds to the number of executable skills from a state, so maximizing empowerment corresponds to reaching states that are good starting points for many skills. Our recipe applies to arbitrary underlying skill learning methods. Whereas most prior work on empowerment looks at tabular settings, this recipe enables us to study empowerment at a scale where we can realize theoretically-predicted but empirically-elusive properties of empowerment (e.g., gathering resources, environment modification, survival). Experiments show that empowerment maximization unlocks interesting emergent properties, such as building a house in Crafter. Website and code at \href{this https URL}{this https url}.

report.summary: A new scalable recipe shows that maximizing empowerment—reaching states with many executable skills—lets agents learn resource gathering, environment modification, and survival at scale.
report.background: Empowerment is an information-theoretic objective in reinforcement learning that measures how much an agent can control its future. Unlike reward maximization, it encourages agents to reach states from which many actions or skills are possible. Prior empowerment research has largely been limited to tabular domains or small state spaces, because estimating and maximizing empowerment at scale is difficult. Skill learning methods, such as unsupervised skill discovery, learn diverse behaviors but do not directly maximize empowerment. This paper bridges that gap by showing empowerment corresponds to the number of executable skills from a state. By scaling this recipe with arbitrary skill-learning methods, the authors can test long-predicted empowerment properties—resource gathering, environment modification, and survival—in richer environments. The work fits broader interest in autonomous, self-directed agents that learn open-ended behaviors without hand-crafted rewards.
key_points: The paper defines empowerment as the number of executable skills available from a state. Maximizing empowerment therefore means steering toward states that are good starting points for many skills, rather than toward a fixed reward. This gives a scalable, skill-based interpretation of an old intrinsic motivation objective and connects it directly to modern skill-learning pipelines.

The proposed recipe is simple and scalable and can wrap around arbitrary skill-learning methods. This matters because prior empowerment work was mostly tabular or small-scale, making theoretically predicted behaviors hard to observe. Scaling lets the authors empirically realize properties such as gathering resources, modifying the environment, and surviving—behaviors that emerge from empowerment maximization rather than explicit reward engineering.

In experiments, empowerment maximization unlocks emergent behavior: the agent builds a house in Crafter. Building a house requires resource collection, crafting, and long-horizon planning, so it serves as a strong demonstration that intrinsic skill-count objectives can produce complex, purposeful-looking outcomes in a challenging open-world benchmark.

The work suggests a path toward generally capable agents that seek optionality and control instead of narrowly optimizing a task reward. It also provides a testbed for studying open-ended learning, skill reuse, and environment modification at a scale where empowerment's theoretical benefits can be measured against practical agent performance.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this work pushes agents away from brittle reward engineering and toward intrinsic objectives that encourage exploration, resource acquisition, and adaptability. Developers can potentially plug the recipe into existing skill-learning stacks to train agents that discover useful behaviors with less task-specific supervision, which may benefit robotics, game AI, and autonomous assistants. For regular users, the near-term effects may appear in more capable NPCs, simulations, and long-horizon assistants that can modify their environments and recover from unexpected situations. However, the experiments are still in benchmarks like Crafter, so production-ready empowerment agents will require robust scaling, safety evaluation, and compute-efficient implementations before they reach consumer products.
report.tools: Start with the paper's official website and code linked in the abstract. Useful environments include Crafter, MiniHack, and Gymnasium for benchmarking; CleanRL or Stable-Baselines3 for RL baselines; and JAX or PyTorch for scalable skill learning. Related methods to watch include DIAYN, EDGE, APT, and quality-diversity/open-ended frameworks. These tools let developers reproduce empowerment maximization and test it with their own skill-learning algorithms.
